name: JavaScript
title: JavaScript (ES2015)
lifecycleNote: Replaced by ES2016 and later editions; engines implement the living standard.

preamble.text: Analysis against ECMAScript 2015 (ECMA-262, 6th edition, June 2015): modules, classes, promises, `let`/`const`, and `Map` are in the standard; `async` functions (ES2017) are not. The family's ES2025 page assesses the current edition.

type.text: **No static types**: the type of a value is whatever the run time finds, so every agreement is deferred to execution
**The call target is chosen from the value**: a property of that name must exist on every object that arrives at the site
**No sum type**: absence is `undefined` or `null`, and an object shape is the alternative encoding, so completeness stays a convention
**No type parameter**: an algorithm over several types duplicates or narrows through one universal value
**Two absence values**: `null` and `undefined` both mean missing, and no signature says a value may be absent
**A signature states no effects**: a call may read a global, write storage, and throw, and the signature names only the return value
**One function kind**: `async` arrives only in ES2017; a generator function suspends, and its caller composes it through iteration rather than by changing kind
**A native addon is an unchecked boundary**: the engine's C ABI is a hand-written declaration that nothing validates
**A host value may arrive later than the call**: a promise composes through `.then`, and the host decides when the value exists
String length and indexing are UTF-16 code-unit operations; charAt can split a surrogate pair

construction.text: **The global object is the default home**: a top-level `var` is a property of the global object, and a forgotten declaration writes there
**Bindings are mutable by default**: nothing states that a property or a variable will not change
**Property order is specified**: the ordinary-key algorithm and `Map`'s insertion order pin the sequence a program prints
**One value, many names**: objects and arrays move by reference, so a parameter, a closure, and a property reach one buffer

memory.text: **A collector reclaims memory**: no release call exists, so a use-after-free is not expressible
**A cycle is not a leak**: a mark-and-sweep collector reclaims objects that point at each other
**A closure holds what it captures**: a listener or a timer keeps its captured objects reachable until it is released
**The collector decides when memory returns**: a pause is the engine's decision, and the program cannot schedule it
**No scope runs a release**: no destructor exists, so a resource is freed in a `finally` or by a convention
**No handle names its owner**: any two references reach the same mutable object

error.text: **A throw is a value**: a failure is caught as an object at the frame that handles it
**A failure may arrive undeclared**: a thrown value needs no signature entry, and no caller is required to handle it
**A failure can be dropped**: an error-first callback may ignore its error argument, and nothing forces the decision
**Each script and each Worker is its own boundary**: an uncaught error ends that script or Worker, not the page's other scripts

concurrency.text: **One event loop**: a long task blocks every other callback, so a CPU-bound computation has no second core
**Shared state is the default**: a global or a captured object is reachable from every callback
**Nothing detects a race**: interleaving is the program's discipline, and no tool checks it
**No scope joins a task**: a callback or a timer can outlive the code that started it
**Promises are values in the standard**: composition and sequencing are expressed in the language

platform.text: **No vendor owns the language**: ECMAScript is standardised by Ecma International as ECMA-262
**Independent engines implement it**: V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore are separate implementations
**Every browser ships an engine, and Node.js runs the language outside the browser**: the source is portable between hosts

performance.text: **A JIT compiles the hot path**: the engine optimizes the code that runs, so a loop is not interpreted statement by statement for long
**The collector's pauses reach the event loop**: a pause delays every pending callback
**The event loop serves I/O**: many pending operations are handled without a thread per operation

ecosystem.text: **A package registry exists**: npm records, fetches, and resolves a project's dependencies
**A native addon binds to the engine's release**: the addon is built against one major and must be rebuilt for another [@nodeAbiStability]

evolution.text: **The TC39 process is public**: a proposal passes fixed stages before it ships
**The language is backward compatible**: an edition adds syntax and keeps the meaning of what it had
**The syntax of the era shapes the code**: module and class syntax arrive with this release, so the code written before it is functions and object literals

domain.text: **The only native browser language**: a user interface that runs in a browser is written in it
**A server runtime runs the same source**: Node.js loads the language outside the browser, so a project shares one language across client and server
**Scripting and glue code**: a short program automates a task or connects two programs
**Poor for systems work**: no control of layout or release timing

learning.text: **A gentle start**: a program runs as soon as it is written, and the browser is the development environment
**`this` follows the call site, and coercion follows the operand**: the two rules a beginner must learn are the two the language explains least

syntax.text: **Object literals and first-class functions express a shape directly**: data and behaviour are written side by side
**Coercion surprises survive reading**: `[] + {}` and `{} + []` differ, and the rule is memorised rather than learned

testing.text: **Test frameworks are mature**: a runner and an assertion library are standard project dependencies
**The engine's developer tools step through the source**: a breakpoint and a call stack are part of every browser
**A mistake is found on the path that runs**: the compiler decides nothing, so coverage is the only evidence of safety

security.text: **A collector removes memory bugs**: a use-after-free and a buffer overflow are not expressible
**A value from outside arrives with no declared type**: keeping it away from a dangerous operation is the programmer's check
**Text becomes code as an ordinary operation**: `eval` parses a string at run time, so a data path can become a control path
Every number is an IEEE-754 double: integers above 2^53 change value in silence, bitwise operators coerce to 32 bits

reproducibility.text: **The lock file pins the graph**: the package manager records resolved versions and verifies them on install
**The interpreter is not pinned by the project**: the language runtime version is left to a version manager or an image

supplychain.text: **The registry records signatures**: a published package carries a verifiable statement of the publisher
**The registry is a flat name space**: a name is a first claim, and a dependency can be redirected without a change in the consumer's source

observability.text: **The instrumentation standard publishes an implementation**: traces and metrics have a stable expressed form

feedback.text: **The edit is the run**: no build step sits between a change and its effect
**An incremental analyser answers as the code is typed**: the editor resolves types and references without a full build

interop.text: **A general foreign-function interface exists**: a native addon calls the platform's C ABI in process

governance.text: **A published conformance suite exists**: Test262 runs against every engine, so the language's meaning is testable outside one implementation
**A published parser exists**: the engine's parser and the compiler API expose the syntax

tradeoffs: **Module syntax vs. loader implementations**: the standard states the module form, and the loader behind it is the host's
**Class syntax vs. the prototype**: the class syntax is a clearer spelling of the same prototype chain, so a reader keeps two vocabularies for one mechanism
**New syntax vs. toolchains**: a project needs a transpiler for the engines that have not shipped the edition
verdict: ES2015 is the edition that turned the language into an application platform. Modules, classes, `let`/`const`, promises, `Map`, and a specified property order arrive together. A module boundary exists at the file level, a specified iteration order replaces the implementation's, and a promise puts asynchronous composition in the language. The type system is still absent, the call target is still chosen at run time, absence is still `null` or `undefined`, and a native addon is still an unchecked boundary. Main strength: the module and class syntax a large application can be built from. Main weakness: nothing in the standard checks a value's type, and the asynchronous function kind that arrives in ES2017 is not yet present.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

use:web-frontend.observation: a user interface that runs in a browser is written in it

use:web-backend.observation: Node.js loads the language outside the browser

use:scripting.observation: a short program automates a task or connects two programs

use:application.observation: Node.js runs the language outside the browser

roleNote: ES5 was a browser scripting language with a young server runtime; the family's shelf follows its current role, so this snapshot records the earlier role and does not move the shelf.

delivery.note: The engine parses the source the package ships
An addon is built against one engine major and must be rebuilt for the next [@nodeAbiStability]
